passages.t: A struggle for people Paul had never met
passages.happening:
“For I want you to know how much I am struggling for you and for those at Laodicea, and for all who have not met me face to face” (verse 1). He wants them “encouraged in heart, knit together in love”, and filled with understanding, “so that they may know the mystery of God, namely Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (verses 2-3).

He says why: “I say this so that no one will deceive you by smooth rhetoric” (verse 4). And though he is far away, he is glad to hear of their “orderly condition and firm faith in Christ” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Paul's ‘struggle’ is the same word he used of his hard labour at the end of chapter 1. For people he has never seen, it is mostly a struggle in prayer, as Epaphras ‘wrestles in prayer’ for them (4:12).

The key words are ‘hidden’ and ‘treasures’. The new teaching seems to have offered hidden knowledge for those who went deeper. Paul says the treasure is not hidden somewhere beyond Christ. It is hidden in Christ. If you want wisdom, you do not need to leave him to find it. You need to dig deeper into him.

‘Smooth rhetoric’ means persuasive talk that sounds right but leads away. Paul is not against clear thinking. He is against fine words that pull people off the gospel they received.

‘Orderly condition’ and ‘firm faith’ can describe soldiers standing in good order, and some readers hear that picture here. The church is holding the line, and Paul is glad.
passages.ot:
Israel's wisdom teachers said wisdom comes from God himself: “For the LORD gives wisdom; from His mouth come knowledge and understanding” (Proverbs 2:6). They told people to search for it “like hidden treasure” (Proverbs 2:4).

Isaiah said the coming King would be filled with it: “The Spirit of the LORD will rest on Him— the Spirit of wisdom and understanding” (Isaiah 11:2). Paul says that wisdom is now found, all of it, in Christ.
passages.asks: Paul says all the treasures of wisdom are hidden in Christ. Ask where you have gone looking for wisdom instead of him. Ask who has struggled in prayer for you without your knowing. And ask whom you could pray for in the same way, even if you have never met them.

passages.t: Complete in Christ: buried, raised, forgiven, set free
passages.happening:
“Therefore, just as you have received Christ Jesus as Lord, continue to walk in Him, rooted and built up in Him, established in the faith as you were taught, and overflowing with thankfulness” (verses 6-7).

The warning: “See to it that no one takes you captive through philosophy and empty deception, which are based on human tradition and the spiritual forces of the world rather than on Christ” (verse 8). The reason: “For in Christ all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form. And you have been made complete in Christ, who is the head over every ruler and authority” (verses 9-10).

Then what they have in him: a circumcision ‘not by human hands’ (verse 11); “having been buried with Him in baptism, you were raised with Him through your faith in the power of God” (verse 12); “God made you alive with Christ. He forgave us all our trespasses, having canceled the debt ascribed to us in the decrees that stood against us. He took it away, nailing it to the cross!” (verses 13-14). “And having disarmed the powers and authorities, He made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them by the cross” (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
Verses 6 and 7 are the heart of the letter: go on as you began. You received Christ; keep walking in him. Paul mixes pictures: a tree with deep roots, a building on a firm base. Both are about staying put in Christ, not moving on from him.

‘Takes you captive’ is a word for carrying someone off as plunder or as a prisoner of war. False teaching can kidnap a believer.

‘Philosophy’ in that world meant a whole way of life, with teaching about the gods, the soul and how to live. The ‘spiritual forces of the world’ translates a word that could mean the basic elements of the world, the first lessons of a subject, or the spirits many believed ruled the elements and the stars. People feared these powers and tried to keep them happy with rituals and rules.

Then verse 9, one of the strongest sentences in the Bible about who Jesus is: ‘all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form’. Not part of God. All of it, in a body. So there is nothing more to find elsewhere.

The pictures pile up. A ‘debt’ was a handwritten note in which a person signed what he owed. God took the note and nailed it to the cross, cancelled. Some readers think of the notice Romans fixed to a cross naming the crime of the one who hung there (John 19:19). And verse 15 is a Roman victory parade, where a general led his defeated enemies through the streets for all to see. At the cross, which looked like Christ's defeat, God put the powers on show as beaten.
passages.ot:
The circumcision ‘not by human hands’ is the circumcision of the heart the law promised: “The LORD your God will circumcise your hearts and the hearts of your descendants, and you will love Him with all your heart” (Deuteronomy 30:6).

The picture of a deeply rooted life is Israel's too: “He is like a tree planted by streams of water, yielding its fruit in season” (Psalm 1:3).

And the forgiveness is the one the prophets and psalms promised: “I have blotted out your transgressions like a cloud, and your sins like a mist. Return to Me, for I have redeemed you” (Isaiah 44:22). “Blessed is he whose transgressions are forgiven, whose sins are covered” (Psalm 32:1).
passages.hard:
Verses 11 and 12 join circumcision and baptism. What do they say about baptism, and whom it is for?

All agree that Paul is speaking of something God does: in Christ, believers are cut free from the old life, buried with Christ and raised with him, and that they are raised ‘through your faith in the power of God’.

Churches read the link with circumcision differently, and these notes do not choose. Presbyterian, Reformed and some other churches see baptism as the sign of the new covenant as circumcision was of the old, given to believers and their children, and many of them read this link between the two signs as one reason for baptizing infants. Catholic, Orthodox and Lutheran churches also baptize infants, and see baptism as God's own work of grace. Baptists, and many other evangelicals, read verse 12's ‘through your faith’ as showing that baptism belongs to those old enough to believe, and see the burial and rising as the picture of believers' immersion. The note on Acts 2:37-41 sets out these views more fully.

What all share is the point Paul makes. Believers need no other mark to belong to God. Christ has given them everything.
passages.asks: Paul says you have been made complete in Christ. Ask what you feel you still need beyond him to be right with God or safe from harm. Ask whether your life is rooted, or easily moved by the latest thing. And picture the record of everything you owe God, nailed to the cross and cancelled. Give thanks.

passages.t: Do not let anyone judge you: the shadow and the reality
passages.happening:
“Therefore let no one judge you by what you eat or drink, or with regard to a feast, a New Moon, or a Sabbath. These are a shadow of the things to come, but the body that casts it belongs to Christ” (verses 16-17).

And: “Do not let anyone who delights in false humility and the worship of angels disqualify you with speculation about what he has seen. Such a person is puffed up without basis by his unspiritual mind” (verse 18). Such a person “has lost connection to the head, from whom the whole body, supported and knit together by its joints and ligaments, grows as God causes it to grow” (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
Food laws, the yearly feasts, the monthly New Moon and the weekly Sabbath were real marks of Jewish life, given by God to Israel. Paul does not call them bad. He calls them a ‘shadow’. A shadow is real. It shows the shape of something. But you do not hug a shadow when the person is standing in front of you. The things these days pointed to have come in Christ.

Some in Colossae were judging believers who did not keep certain rules about food and days, and telling them they were missing out. Paul says no one has the right to judge you on these grounds.

‘Disqualify’ is a word from the games: an umpire ruling someone out. Some claimed special visions and a humble-looking worship that involved angels, and looked down on those who had not seen what they had seen. Scholars debate exactly what ‘the worship of angels’ was: worship given to angels, or a claim to join in the worship angels offer in heaven. Either way, Paul says such people are ‘puffed up’, proud while looking humble.

And they have lost hold of ‘the head’. The church grows as a body grows, from Christ the head, joint by joint. Cut off from the head, all the visions in the world will not make it grow.
passages.ot:
The Sabbath was God's gift from creation: “Then God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, because on that day He rested from all the work of creation” (Genesis 2:3). It was written in the commandments (Exodus 20:8-11), and tied to the freeing of slaves from Egypt (Deuteronomy 5:15).

The prophets warned that holy days could be kept without a holy heart: “your New Moons, Sabbaths, and convocations. I cannot endure iniquity in a solemn assembly” (Isaiah 1:13).

And God sees past outward show: “For man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7).
passages.hard:
Does verse 16 mean Christians should not keep the Sabbath, or any special day?

Christians agree that rest is God's good gift and part of creation, that Jesus is Lord of the Sabbath, that God's people gather to worship, and that the final rest of God's people is still to come. And all agree with Paul's clearest point: keeping or not keeping a day must never be made the ground of anyone's standing with God, or a test to judge others by.

Beyond that they differ, and these notes do not choose. Seventh-day Sabbath keepers hold that the fourth commandment still applies as given, and that Saturday remains the Sabbath for Christians; they read this verse as about special feast-day sabbaths or the teachers' own rules, not the weekly Sabbath of the Ten Commandments. Many Reformed and Presbyterian churches, following the Westminster Confession of 1646, teach that the Sabbath principle continues but has moved to the Lord's Day, Sunday, in honour of the resurrection, to be kept for worship, rest and mercy. Others, including many Lutherans, Baptists and other evangelicals, hold that the Sabbath command was a sign of the old covenant fulfilled in Christ, so believers rest in him rather than keeping a day as law, while still valuing regular worship and rest. Paul says elsewhere, “One person regards a certain day above the others, while someone else considers every day alike. Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind” (Romans 14:5).

The site's wisdom topic on rest and Sabbath sets out these views as well.
passages.asks: Paul says no one should judge you over food and days, or rule you out over visions. Ask whether you have judged other believers by rules Christ did not give. Ask whether you have let someone else's spiritual experience make you feel second-class. And ask whether you are holding on to the head.

passages.t: Rules that look wise and cannot change the heart
passages.happening:
“If you have died with Christ to the spiritual forces of the world, why, as though you still belonged to the world, do you submit to its regulations: ‘Do not handle, do not taste, do not touch!’?” (verses 20-21).

These rules are about things that “will all perish with use, because they are based on human commands and teachings” (verse 22).

“Such restrictions indeed have an appearance of wisdom, with their self-prescribed worship, their false humility, and their harsh treatment of the body; but they are of no value against the indulgence of the flesh” (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
‘Do not handle, do not taste, do not touch’ sounds like a list of rules piling up, each stricter than the last. Paul may be quoting the teachers' own slogans.

His argument is simple. You died with Christ. The powers and rules of the old world no longer own you. So why live as though they still did?

And notice that Paul is fair to these rules. He admits they ‘have an appearance of wisdom’. Strict rules, hard self-denial and harsh treatment of the body can look very holy. People admire them. But they cannot do what they promise. They do not change the heart. A person can keep every rule and still be ruled by pride, anger or greed. That is why the next chapter turns from rules to a new life in Christ.

This is not an attack on self-control, fasting or simple living. Jesus fasted, and Paul disciplined his own body (1 Corinthians 9:27). It is an attack on rules made up by people and treated as the way to God, rules that make people proud and leave the heart untouched.
passages.ot:
Isaiah spoke against religion that is only outward: “These people draw near to Me with their mouths and honor Me with their lips, but their hearts are far from Me. Their worship of Me is but rules taught by men” (Isaiah 29:13). Jesus quoted those words against human rules about washing (Mark 7:6-7).

And God told Israel what kind of fasting he wanted: not only bowing the head, but “to break the chains of wickedness, to untie the cords of the yoke, to set the oppressed free” (Isaiah 58:6).
passages.asks: Paul says rules can look wise and still leave the heart unchanged. Ask what rules you keep that make you feel better than others. Ask whether your self-discipline has made you humbler or prouder. And ask what in your heart no rule has been able to change, and bring it to Christ.
